[Sample 243]
“Why do you want to relocate?”

It’s one of the most common interview questions international job seekers get, and one where your answer can quietly hurt your chances of moving forward.

Many candidates answer it by talking almost exclusively about wanting to move abroad, seeking a better quality of life, higher salaries, and the like.

Here’s the problem: when that’s your entire answer, you unintentionally shift the focus away from the one thing the recruiter actually wants to hear about: the company.

By the time you’re sitting in that interview, they already know you want to relocate.

What they really want to hear is that you’re genuinely excited about joining their team.

In my latest article for The Global Move, I explain:

- why focusing so much on the idea of relocating during interviews can work against you;
- what employers actually want to hear instead; and
- how to approach relocation questions the right way, with examples of weak and strong answers.

Hope it comes in handy for those of you who are currently looking for a tech job abroad.

Check out the article here 👇

https://relocateme.substack.com/p/a-mistake-to-avoid-during-relocation

How will searching for a tech job with relocation look in 2026?

From what we’re seeing running The Global Move and Relocate.me, it will be:

• more competitive
• more global
• more dependent on strategy

… than in previous years, especially if you compare against, let’s say, 2021.

More specifically:

1️⃣ 
There will be no “easier market” to move to. Mature tech hubs will stay competitive, and emerging ones will quickly attract global talent.

2️⃣ 
Over-application will break the traditional application model. Sending more applications won’t necessarily increase your chances. Precision will matter much, much more than volume.

3️⃣
Getting to the first interview will require multiple entry points: direct application, recruiter outreach, referrals, visibility (content, open source, community presence), to name a few. Oftentimes, even for one role.

4️⃣
Being findable will matter as much as applying. Candidates who share projects, write, contribute, and show clear expertise will have a higher chance of being approached rather than ignored.

5️⃣
Referrals will continue to be one of the most effective ways to get interviews. But the nature of referrals will change. This year, cold messages like “Can you refer me?” will rarely work.

We’ve broken all of this down in more detail (plus five other predictions) in our new Substack post.

“Why do you want to relocate?”

It’s one of the most common interview questions international job seekers get, and one where your answer can quietly hurt your chances of moving forward.

Many candidates answer it by talking almost exclusively about wanting to move abroad, seeking a better quality of life, higher salaries, and the like.

Here’s the problem: when that’s your entire answer, you unintentionally shift the focus away from the one thing the recruiter actually wants to hear about: the company.

By the time you’re sitting in that interview, they already know you want to relocate.

What they really want to hear is that you’re genuinely excited about joining their team.

In my latest article for The Global Move, I explain:

- why focusing so much on the idea of relocating during interviews can work against you;
- what employers actually want to hear instead; and
- how to approach relocation questions the right way, with examples of weak and strong answers.

Hope it comes in handy for those of you who are currently looking for a tech job abroad.

Check out the article here 👇

https://relocateme.substack.com/p/a-mistake-to-avoid-during-relocation

How will searching for a tech job with relocation look in 2026?

From what we’re seeing running The Global Move and Relocate.me, it will be:

• more competitive
• more global
• more dependent on strategy

… than in previous years, especially if you compare against, let’s say, 2021.

More specifically:

1️⃣ 
There will be no “easier market” to move to. Mature tech hubs will stay competitive, and emerging ones will quickly attract global talent.

2️⃣ 
Over-application will break the traditional application model. Sending more applications won’t necessarily increase your chances. Precision will matter much, much more than volume.

3️⃣
Getting to the first interview will require multiple entry points: direct application, recruiter outreach, referrals, visibility (content, open source, community presence), to name a few. Oftentimes, even for one role.

4️⃣
Being findable will matter as much as applying. Candidates who share projects, write, contribute, and show clear expertise will have a higher chance of being approached rather than ignored.

5️⃣
Referrals will continue to be one of the most effective ways to get interviews. But the nature of referrals will change. This year, cold messages like “Can you refer me?” will rarely work.

We’ve broken all of this down in more detail (plus five other predictions) in our new Substack post.
